entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during thunderstorms that lasts a few seconds and then vanishes, with or without a trace. It has no agreed explanation.
entries.background: Reported for centuries by thousands of eyewitnesses, but almost never captured by instruments, so scientists still debate whether and how it forms.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist whose 1837 work on thunder is where the term 'ball lightning' is traced to. He collected reports of such sightings.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: German school official who wrote 'Der Kugelblitz' (1923), a monograph on ball lightning and the only one in German.

entries.name: Martin A. Uman
entries.background: American lightning researcher at the University of Florida. He co-wrote a standard handbook on lightning and led rocket-triggered lightning experiments at Camp Blanding.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Russian physics professor who keeps a database of ball lightning cases and co-edited a book on the phenomenon.

entries.name: fragmented science
entries.senseHere: A description of ball lightning research as scattered effort. Some people collect reports, some build theories, and others run lab tests, with little coordination.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: The Austrian network of sensors that locates lightning strokes and records their strength and polarity.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: The German lightning location service that detects where and when lightning strikes.

entries.name: positive lightning stroke
entries.background: A lightning discharge that carries positive electric charge to the ground. It is much rarer than the negative kind but often more powerful.

entries.name: cloud–ground stroke
entries.background: A lightning bolt that travels between a thundercloud and the ground, as opposed to one that stays between clouds.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist and member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at the Göttingen university observatory who reported a childhood ball lightning sighting to Nature.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: American palaeontologist at Yale, known for dinosaur fossil discoveries, and president of the US National Academy of Sciences.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German experimental physicist, famous for the 1922 Stern–Gerlach experiment showing that atoms' magnetic orientation comes in fixed steps.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer who later became a professor of physical electronics. He wrote a widely noticed account in Nature of a glowing sphere passing through an airliner cabin.

entries.name: Pikes Peak
entries.background: A 4302 m summit in Colorado's Rocky Mountains where the Harvard College Observatory ran a weather station in the 1870s and 1880s.

entries.name: Puy de Dôme
entries.background: A 1465 m extinct volcano in the Massif Central of France with a weather observatory on its summit.

entries.name: Mt Sonnblick
entries.background: A 3106 m peak in the Austrian province of Salzburg with a summit weather observatory.

entries.name: Mt Fichtelberg
entries.background: A 1215 m mountain in Saxony, Germany with a meteorological observatory.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist at the St Petersburg Academy who was killed by lightning in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: Short-lived paralysis and numbness after a lightning strike or ball lightning encounter, which Charcot separated from lasting nervous trauma.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician who founded modern neurology and taught at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris. Sigmund Freud studied under him and translated his lectures.

entries.name: Dorstone case
entries.background: A 1936 report from Herefordshire, England, of a red-hot ball that fell into a water tub and made it boil. It is used to estimate how much energy a ball holds.

entries.name: Poughquag case
entries.background: A 2008 sighting in New York State of a blue ball seen through a glass porch door. Later measurements of the glass's glow estimated the ball's radiation output.

entries.name: Camp Blanding experiment
entries.background: A 2008 field experiment in Florida in which rocket-launched wires triggered lightning onto more than 100 ground materials, which were then photographed and analysed.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.background: A 2012 recording on the Qinghai Plateau in China in which cameras with diffraction gratings captured the light spectrum of a ball lightning object.

entries.name: Mitino incident
entries.background: A 2015 Moscow event in which three people filmed a glowing object with mobile phones. Triangulating the films gave its height and speed.
